newsitem.title: CHINA: China says hopes for end to Korea defector crisis.
newsitem.headline: China says hopes for end to Korea defector crisis.

text.p: China said on Tuesday it hoped a solution could be found to a three-week defector crisis centred on South Korea's Beijing mission but gave no hint as to when the most senior leader to flee North Korea would be able to leave.

Top North Korean ideological theoretician Hwang Jang-yop has been marooned in Seoul's consular compound in Beijing since February 12, surrounded by a Chinese police cordon backed by armoured personnel carriers and an anti-riot truck.
China remained hopeful that a resolution to the three-way diplomatic crisis sparked by Hwang's defection could be found, Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang said.
"We hope the relevant sides can deal with the matter appropriately on the basis of safeguarding peace and stability on the Korean peninsula," Tang told a news briefing.

"We hope that this matter will not affect relations between the relevant sides," he said. He declined to comment on when Hwang might be able to leave his high-security sanctuary in Beijing's tree-lined diplomatic quarter.

South Korean sources say the crisis could drag on for some time and Seoul on Monday hinted that talks with China over Hwang's fate were being held back while Beijing was busy with its annual session of parliament.
The full session of the National People's Congress opened on Saturday. It will sit for two weeks.
"We did not get any resolution from the Chinese government so far," embassy spokesman Chang Moon-ik said on Monday. "I think they are very busy because the national assembly is going on."

In his annual government work report made to the opening session of the congress on Saturday, Chinese Premier Li Peng made no mention of the crisis but said Beijing hoped for stability on the Korean peninsula.
Beijing has been a reluctant participant in the showdown between Pyongyang and Seoul, forced to choose between offending an old communist comrade or a new capitalist friend.
Analysts say China is almost certain to grant Hwang, a senior aide to top leader Kim Jong-Il and the architect of North Korea's governing ideology of strict self-reliance, safe passage to Seoul.
But Beijing wants to help its hermit neighbour save face by being seen to give weight to Pyongyang's concerns, they say.
North and South Korea remain technically at war after their 1950-53 conflict ended with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
